Understanding SQLite WAL Mode

Published March 11, 2024

By default SQLite uses a rollback journal: every write first copies the original pages to the journal, then modifies the database file in place. Write-ahead logging inverts that. Changes are appended to a separate wal file first, and readers keep working against the original database while writers commit. See the official WAL documentation for the full details. You can enable it with the inline pragma PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL on any open connection.

How checkpoints work

A checkpoint moves committed frames from the wal file back into the main database. It runs automatically once the log grows past a threshold, and it never blocks readers.

  • Readers never block writers, and writers never block readers.
    • Even long-running read transactions keep a consistent snapshot.
  • Checkpointing can run concurrently with ongoing reads.
  • All processes accessing the database must be on the same host.

WAL mode is safe for concurrent access by multiple processes on the same host, which is exactly the deployment hube targets.

For an embedded server workload, the trade is straightforward: slightly more disk usage for the log, in exchange for readers that never wait.
